# Decoding Engine Temperature and Thermostat Logic

The assertion that automotive engines are universally designed to operate at exactly 212°F (100°C) under all external conditions is a common misconception often found in generalist discussions like those on Bob the Oil Guy. While running hot does improve thermal efficiency and reduce emissions by ensuring complete combustion, modern engine management systems prioritize maintaining a stable operating window rather than hitting a single target number regardless of ambient temperature or load.

In your specific case with the 1997 Mazda 323 BA equipped with an 82.5°C thermostat, observing temperatures between 85°C and 92°C is not necessarily indicative of a failure. The discrepancy arises from how you are interpreting the data versus how the cooling loop physically behaves. A thermostat rated at 82.5°C typically opens fully within a few degrees above that rating to allow coolant flow through the radiator. However, this does not mean the water will instantly drop to 82.5°C once the valve cracks open; it means heat transfer begins aggressively.

The ECU reading you are seeing represents the average thermal state of the engine block and cylinder head sensors, which respond slower than surface temperature spikes. When driving at steady speed or in stop-and-go traffic where the fan cycles on at 97°C, the system is likely cycling between the thermostat opening (restricting flow to keep heat up) and full open (dissipating excess heat). If your coolant mixture adheres strictly to the manufacturer's recommendation of 65% water and 35% glycol-ethylene concentrate for environments above -15°C, you are managing the boiling point correctly. Adding extra coolant without water can actually lower the specific heat capacity of the fluid, potentially causing faster temperature swings if the system is already running slightly lean on flow.

A critical factor here is the non-OEM radiator and the use of a thermostat that may differ from the factory specification. The original equipment manufacturer (OEM) likely selected a thermostat opening point optimized for your specific water-cooling capacity. Replacing it with an 82.5°C unit might be too aggressive for a stock cooling system, forcing the fan to work harder than necessary to dump heat once the valve opens fully. This explains why you see the temperature spike to 97°C before the fan engages; the thermostat held back flow until the liquid reached its maximum safe limit relative to the new valve's opening curve.

From an engineering perspective, this scenario mirrors writing a control loop with tight PID gains that oscillate rather than settling. The "normal" operating range for many gasoline engines, particularly those from the late 90s era of your Mazda, is often cited between 85°C and 95°C. Pushing toward 100°C was more common in high-performance or European applications where thermal efficiency was prioritized over longevity under all conditions. Your current readings suggest the engine is running warm enough to minimize oil thinning but not so hot as to risk detonation or head gasket failure, provided it rarely exceeds 105°C.

If you wish to verify the system's true behavior, monitor the temperature gauge during a cold start in winter versus summer. A healthy loop should stabilize quickly after the thermostat opens. If the needle bounces violently between low and high marks without settling, that indicates air pockets or a failing water pump rather than just thermostat calibration issues. Ultimately, unless the engine is overheating (above 105°C) or running dangerously cold (below 75°C in hot climates), an operating range of 85°C to 92°C with your modified thermostat is functionally acceptable for daily driving, even if it deviates from the theoretical "design point" often quoted in literature.
